title: The City Beneath the Recitation
summary: Textual scholarship exposes a temple’s layered foundations while a household revival confronts the memory of mass confinement.
source_notes: Philological comparison and questioning a single author become the study of layered founding recitations.
Household-led religious meetings and a declared state of perfection become a movement promising release from inherited guilt.

entries.title: Orvel the Unenrolled Reader
entries.body:
Orvel registered as a comparison reader before the temple school recognized that occupation. Refused formal lectures, he copied masons’ marks instead. His pupils now control admission to a prestigious chair and are debating whether to repeat the exclusion that formed his method.

Later accounts make Orvel the Unenrolled Reader the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The City Beneath the Recitation. Sere’s oldest inland temple was repeatedly rebuilt as river silt raised the surrounding ground. Its custodians recited a single founding poem, although repairs preserved portions of older and contradictory versions. In 903, suspicion of coastal ancestry led Vey’s council to confine thousands of residents in dry compounds. Their former neighbors acquired abandoned workshops. A household prayer movement later promised release from inherited guilt through a simple declaration made beside water. A scholar comparing temple recitations argued that neither the city’s origin nor its wrongdoing could be reduced to one speaker and one cleansing act. His evidence joined the displaced families’ claims to foundations the council called sacred.

In the connected record, [The Temple of Lower Steps](b004-the-temple-of-lower-steps.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Separate Restitution Clause](b004-the-separate-restitution-clause.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether a public act of repentance will restore workshop access or merely authorize the present owners to feel absolved.
entries.background: Vey households measure wealth partly in dependable access to a public landing. Their markets exchange grain, lamp oil, glazed jars, and legal testimony. A witness can authenticate a transaction but cannot provide the labor needed to fulfill it. Seasonal crews clean the same embankments on which courts announce judgments, and a decision that ignores those crews soon meets an expensive physical limit. Flood deposits preserve small objects while destroying the arrangement that once made their meaning obvious. Recovering an object is therefore easier than establishing what anybody was entitled to do with it.

entries.title: The Temple of Lower Steps
entries.body:
Each rebuilding concealed an older stair beneath a higher floor. Pilgrims praise ascent, while drainage workers descend to keep foundations dry. The lowest tread preserves a promise to feed river arrivals absent from the current public recitation.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Tuesday Basin Houses
entries.body:
Household meetings let women and servants testify without a temple credential. Their leaders promise freedom from ancestral guilt. Some households treat that promise as permission to retain workshops acquired during confinement, turning a liberating practice into protection for an old advantage.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Dry Compound Removal
entries.body:
Officials removed residents with coastal grandparents while exempting valuable interpreters of the same ancestry. Their inconsistent exemptions reveal an administrative choice, not an unavoidable response to danger. A surviving cart account identifies neighbors who profited from vacated rooms.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Lowest Step Tile
entries.body:
A loosened tile records a meal obligation in an archaic script. Temple officials claim it belongs to an unrelated building. Its mortar matches the earliest stair, while its food quantities align with old landing accounts, making dismissal increasingly difficult.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Declaration of Clear Hands
entries.body:
Participants wash once and declare themselves free to act without inherited guilt. Displaced descendants ask them to return keys afterward. The division between moral relief and practical restitution has fractured meetings that once welcomed the same households.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Founding Poem in Nine Voices
entries.body:
Orvel’s edition places variant lines beside one another instead of choosing a smooth original. Readers hear contradictory obligations as distinct historical layers. The temple fears this weakens reverence, while cooks say it finally acknowledges changes their provisioning records always showed.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Stairwell Glass Snail
entries.body:
Translucent snails gather along seepage beneath the temple. Cleaners remove them before festivals, erasing clues to damaged mortar. Apprentices map their return and use that pattern to find a leak older diviners had attributed to offended founders.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Compound Return Lane
entries.body:
Former detainees returned along a lane lined with workshops occupied by neighbors. The council arranged a welcome ceremony but issued no keys. Descendants retrace the lane carrying repair tools, asking whether return means physical arrival or restored ability to earn a living.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Separate Restitution Clause
entries.body:
The clause distinguishes pardon, repentance, and return of property. None automatically performs the others. Patrons support its moral language but oppose inspection of their rents. Petitioners now request separate written decisions for each issue so one favorable phrase cannot conceal two refusals.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Festival of One Clean Day
entries.body:
A citywide cleansing festival briefly united restitution campaigners and present workshop owners. Afterward, rents remained unchanged. The next year campaigners set up an account table beside the basin, asking celebrants to record a specific action rather than repeat a declaration.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Compound Door Weights
entries.body:
Iron weights from confinement gates became temple bell counterweights. Their provenance emerged during repairs. Some custodians want them removed to restore purity; displaced families want them retained with accurate labels, keeping the sanctuary’s comfort connected to its civic history.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: Meals Below the Recitation
entries.body:
Volunteers revive the lowest stair’s food obligation for river arrivals. The temple accepts the meals but refuses the volunteers a place in its festival. They maintain separate accounts to prevent their labor becoming evidence for the custodians’ claimed generosity.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Keys Not Returned
entries.body:
This booklet pairs welcome speeches with unresolved workshop claims. Its compiler avoids saying every present owner is guilty, which disappoints some campaigners. Precise ownership histories nevertheless make it harder for officials to dismiss the whole collection as indiscriminate accusation.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Basin That Will Not Clear
entries.body:
Water clouds after clear-hands ceremonies when drainage below the temple backs up. Some participants call this rejection of repentance. Repair records link the clouding to festival crowds, leaving a practical fault whose correction cannot decide the separate question of restitution.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Mortar Reading
entries.body:
Masons distinguish successive repairs through lime, grit, and tool impressions. Their expertise makes them valuable historical witnesses. Readers who once ignored manual labor now compete for their services, and apprentices demand named credit rather than anonymous inclusion in a scholar’s conclusions.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Ninth Voice Petition
entries.body:
A variant recitation grants arrivals access to kilns for one firing season. Descendants invoke it against exclusive clay rights. The court must decide whether restoring the old obligation requires a present cooperative schedule or the impossible reconstruction of an extinct household.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
